summary.text:
Powys's DRAFT Capital and Treasury Management Strategy 2026-31 (Appendix H, Finance Panel 30 January 2026) sets out an ambitious five-year borrowing trajectory almost entirely driven by the HRA. CFR nearly doubles from £443m at 31 March 2025 to £842m by 31 March 2031, with HRA CFR growing 150% (£126m → £315m) against a Council Fund CFR growth of only 54%.

The standout indicator is the HRA financing cost ratio: 18.5% in 2025/26 rising to 35.9% by 2030/31 — the highest endpoint we have read. By 2030/31, one pound in three of HRA rental income will be servicing debt. Debt per dwelling rises 83% to £51,338. The driver is Welsh Housing Quality Standard 2023, which Powys itself states (§1.46) 'is not affordable while retaining social rents within the limits set by the WG' — the target cost is £179m excluding financing.

The borrowing strategy (§1.94) is built on a rate view that has not held. The MUFG August 2025 forecast projected 5yr PWLB falling from 4.80% (Sep-25) to 4.30% (Sep-26); certainty rates are around 5.34% today, up 0.39% since 30 September 2025. Rates have moved the opposite way to the forecast — and the paper explicitly allowed for drawing fixed if that happened (§1.95 second bullet).

Internal borrowing is a moving target: the Portfolio Position table (§1.93) and the Change in External Debt table (§1.112) give different 31-March-2026 estimates for external debt (£334.75m vs £407.25m), implying either £132.5m or £60m of internal borrowing depending on which path Powys actually follows. The £72.5m gap between them is the amount of new borrowing the plan assumes but debt run-off implies won't happen.

The loan-book reconciliation did not tie cleanly. Our file holds 122 PWLB loans at £256.97m at 2026-03-31 — within 0.57% of the paper's PWLB actual at 31 March 2025 (£255.51m) but £25m off the 31 March 2026 estimate (£231.97m). Because our bc-loans Start field is not a reliable drawdown date and the as-at 2025-03-31 lookup returns empty, we cannot assert the tie is real. The claim is out of the email; the gap is here.

One other feature worth noting: £109m (30% of external debt) is 'Market/Other Local Authorities', a large intra-LA position for a rural Welsh unitary. §1.102 says local-authority borrowing 'primarily out to 3 years or so' remains cheaper than the Certainty Rate.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on your draft Capital and Treasury Management Strategy 2026-31 that went to Finance Panel on 30 January and then on to Council in February. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your strategy is unusually thorough for its length, and this is offered in that spirit rather than as a critique.

The number that stopped us was in paragraph 1.105. Your HRA financing-cost-to-net-revenue-stream ratio is 18.5% in 2025/26, and by 2030/31 you have it at 35.9%. Of the councils we have read, that endpoint is the highest we've seen — over one pound in three of HRA rental income going to service debt by the end of the plan. HRA financing costs rise from £5.93m to £13.63m over five years (up 130%), while the net revenue stream grows just £5.90m (up 18%). It is a striking piece of arithmetic to have put in front of members.

The driver is the Welsh Housing Quality Standard 2023 investment your paragraph 1.46 costs at £179m excluding financing. HRA CFR grows from £126m to £315m — up 150% in five years — and debt per dwelling from £28,066 in 2026/27 to £51,338 by 2030/31, an 83% increase. Your paper itself says the WHQS-2023 investment "is not affordable while retaining social rents within the limits set by the WG". That sentence is unusually plain about the constraint, and it is worth having the financing side sit alongside it in the same conversation.

On the borrowing strategy itself, paragraph 1.94 sets out the case for continuing under-borrowed on the view that "medium and longer dated borrowing rates are expected to fall from their current levels". The MUFG forecast in Appendix D (dated 11 August 2025) has 5-year PWLB going from 4.80% at Sep-25 to 4.30% by Sep-26 and to 4.10% by Sep-28. Today, on notice 314/26, the 5-year certainty rate is 5.34% — about 0.39% above where it was at your 30 September 2025 reference point in the Appendix C/D chart. Across the curve rates are up roughly a third of a point since then. Not an accusation; your paragraph 1.95 explicitly allowed for drawing fixed if rates spiked. It is now a testable assumption with an answer, and the answer is worth reading against your capital-programme funding gap.

That gap is quite large on the current path. Reading your paragraph 1.93 portfolio table forward from £367.63m of external debt at 31 March 2025 to £334.75m at 31 March 2026, debt drops by £33m as existing loans mature. But the CFR runs the other way — up £24m in 2025/26 alone, then £63m, £98m, £86m, £74m, £54m across the following years. That leaves the difference to be filled either by new borrowing (your paragraph 1.112 has it at £44m in 2025/26 and £83m in 2026/27) or by drawing further on internal balances. On the portfolio table you finish 2025/26 with implied internal borrowing of about £132m against a CFR of £467m; on the change-in-debt table it is £60m. That £72m spread between the two versions is essentially the size of the strategy decision that is now live.

The liability benchmark is the tool that visualises exactly this: what your existing debt is doing, what your CFR needs, and where the gap has to be filled. Your paragraph 1.75 has the chart itself. We built an interactive version of the liability-benchmark pathway that runs live off our data — you can drop in your existing book and see the shape month by month. CIPFA is refreshing the Prudential and Treasury Codes and the liability benchmark sits at the heart of that update. Ours is at pwlbtoday.org/liability-benchmark.

A smaller thing worth mentioning. Your paragraph 1.93 shows £109.00m of market and other-local-authority borrowing at 31 March 2025 — 30% of your external debt. Estimated to fall to £100m by 31 March 2026, so a chunk of it is short-dated. Your paragraph 1.102 explains the reason: LA borrowing out to about three years remains cheaper than the Certainty Rate. That market has been running much wider than usual this year: we've seen it at anything from about 4.15% to 8.50% depending on who needed money and when, with volume rising as well — Staffordshire's lending book went from £30m to £152m across twenty-five councils, and Liverpool raised £118m of two-to-four-year money from seventeen. Whether you're at the borrower or lender end, that spread widening changes the maths. It's at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

One piece of honest disclosure. We tried to tie our PWLB file to your paragraph 1.93 and cannot say it holds. Our file at your March 2026 date has 122 loans totalling £256.97m at a weighted 3.59%. Your PWLB actual at March 2025 is £255.51m — close, within 0.57% — but your March 2026 estimate is £231.97m and we are £25m clear of that. Rather than quote either figure, we'll leave it and revisit when you publish the outturn.

On training, four fit the shape of your strategy. HRA business planning goes to paragraph 1.105 and the 35.9% ratio. Interest rate risk goes to your paragraph 1.94 view and the market's answer. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets goes to your £109m position. Liability benchmark goes to your paragraph 1.75 chart. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find any of it useful, mentioning it to others in Wales would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Source: DRAFT Capital Strategy and Treasury Management Strategy 2026-31 (Appendix H), Finance Panel 30 January 2026 — https://powys.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s102150/appendix-h-capital-and-treasury-management-strategy-2026-31.pdf
